section.title: Technical excellence needs a clear user and a useful problem
section.deck: Adam Ernst explains code-driven influence, successful iOS infrastructure, and the lessons from a technically accomplished framework that failed to gain adoption.

blocks.question: What was your middle-school software company?
answer: Ernst began programming young, spending time with computers in his teacher mother’s classroom. His first commercial product was online-testing software, sold internationally through a cross-platform BASIC-inspired development tool. He remembers the project as an accessible way to make something useful, despite the tool’s limitations.

followups.question: What made the development environment accessible?
answer: A drag-and-drop canvas let him place buttons and fields directly, then attach code to interactions. Unlike writing a textual UI description first, that immediate visual feedback was easy for a beginner. It was less suited to scaling large applications, but suitable for his first product.

followups.question: How did you sell software internationally before modern payment APIs?
answer: An existing software-store service handled cards and license-unlock codes. He also accepted mailed checks from teachers and emailed their codes back. The service name is uncertain in the captions and is not essential to the example.

followups.question: Did your parents know?
answer: Yes. He is unsure what they thought, but says they knew about the business.

blocks.question: What did you join Facebook to do, and at what level?
answer: He believes he joined as E5 because of prior self-employed iPhone development experience, arriving shortly before the 2012 IPO. The iOS engineering group was still small enough to meet in one room. Its rewrite from an HTML5 approach to native code had won organizational support, creating both opportunities and scaling problems as new features accumulated.

blocks.question: What storage problem drove your staff-level work?
answer: The native rewrite used Apple’s Core Data, which Ernst considers useful for a small application team but unsuitable for their rapidly expanding organization. As the engineering group grew from roughly fifteen or twenty to hundreds, product teams wanted native features while the infrastructure team feared the storage layer would fail.

The migration had to be incremental because feature work could not simply stop. Their new immutable model system made mutation and thread-safety reasoning easier. His account illustrates a scaling constraint involving both technical architecture and the number of teams sharing it.

followups.question: Why was adoption difficult?
answer: Core products such as feed had obvious performance gains, but the remaining teams sometimes saw little benefit compared with their other priorities. Some iOS engineers also strongly preferred built-in Apple frameworks. Ernst had to repeatedly explain the particular limits at Facebook’s scale rather than assume everyone valued replacement for its own sake.

blocks.question: How can an IC influence other engineers without formal authority?
answer: Speak in person or over video when possible; nuance and tone can be easier to convey than in writing. Begin sympathetically: he too would prefer standard Apple frameworks if they solved the problem. Then provide concrete evidence of why they do not.

The team investigated Core Data’s otherwise opaque implementation, including disassembly, to explain initialization costs. Research gave the argument more substance than a preference for a new framework.

He also often performed migration work himself. Asking someone to approve a completed improvement is easier than asking them to spend their own time adopting scaffolding. He qualifies the tactic: Meta’s later codebase became too large for one person to finish such migrations, making broader alignment more necessary.

blocks.question: Why spend so much time reviewing code?
answer: Code review supplies a concrete opening for influencing engineering habits. Ernst can discuss an actual design rather than issue an abstract company-wide message. He tries to explain concerns flexibly, allowing a reasonable differing choice or helping the author make a necessary change. Authors who understand the reasoning may carry it into their future work and their own reviews, spreading the influence organically.

followups.question: What makes a good review comment?
answer: Explain why a change matters instead of merely ordering X to become Y. Admit that context may be missing and ask whether it would change the recommendation. If it does, encourage including that context in the diff summary so others can review the decision on its merits. Flexibility does not mean abandoning concerns; it means making them intelligible and revisable.

blocks.question: Why did you build ComponentKit?
answer: Around 2014, rapidly growing news-feed code suffered crashes, layout errors, and performance problems. Ernst credits Lee Byron with asking how React’s concepts could work in an iOS-oriented form. ComponentKit was his response.

It used components, immutability, conceptual re-rendering, and view reconciliation. Instead of manually coordinating view objects, product code declared what should appear and the framework managed the native views. He is proud of the balance among syntax, performance, and the business need.

The work included inventing the framework, introducing it into feed, and spreading it to other products. He places it before the later mainstream SwiftUI and React Native options in the historical context he remembers.

followups.question: How did you convince engineers to adopt an unfamiliar declarative model?
answer: Examples showed much less code; performance demonstrations showed work moving off the main thread. Some engineers remained unconvinced, so more senior engineers helped mediate. React’s established reputation internally also helped. Ernst acknowledged awkwardness in the Objective-C++ approach rather than deny its costs, and repeatedly explained the benefits for this application.

followups.question: What general lessons did the disagreements teach?
answer: Allies could persuade in ways his own style could not. Compromise also mattered: another team’s Panels framework was meant to be the next UI direction, and the overlap was painful. Incorporating part of its data-source technology into ComponentKit created a shared win. He recommends bringing people into the solution rather than insist on every detail being his own.

blocks.question: Did strong pushback make you doubt ComponentKit?
answer: He remained convinced for news feed, while rejecting it as the only acceptable UI architecture. A mostly static scrolling list with complicated nested content suited declarative rendering. A highly dynamic drag-and-drop interface might feel much less natural. Conviction about the intended application coexisted with awareness of paradigm tradeoffs.

blocks.question: Why build ComponentScript, and what happened?
answer: The next ambition was cross-platform UI without separately writing iOS and Android versions. In Ernst’s opinion, React Native at that time worked better when it controlled an app than when small cross-platform pieces were embedded throughout a complex native app. He explicitly leaves open that later architectural changes improved this.

His first attempt to implement React above the existing native frameworks proved too difficult because React’s surface was large and complex. A smaller React-like JavaScript API became ComponentScript. It supported real features, full screens, and nested native and scripted components.

The project nevertheless failed after about two years. It satisfied the infrastructure group’s technical requirements but did not generate enough sustained adoption. He distinguishes a working implementation from a successful offering.

followups.question: What did the postmortem identify?
answer: It had no clear target engineer. iOS developers did not want to learn JavaScript, while JavaScript developers preferred actual React Native to an unfamiliar React-like API.

He insisted on GraphQL-based data consistency, but its tooling was slow at the time. A competing server-driven approach could skip that burden for products that did not require consistency and handle the exceptional cases individually. He sees his refusal to compromise as part of the failure.

He also approached many individual engineers rather than securing one committed team. Scattered experiments did not build momentum. A team finally wanted broad adoption when he was ending the effort, but he believes that was already too little and too late.

blocks.question: Why publish such a candid retrospective?
answer: Writing it was cathartic, answered repeated questions about the project, and explained the failure once without continually reliving the conversation. He hoped others would recognize the same traps before repeating them. He does not clearly remember whether someone also encouraged him to write it.

blocks.question: How did the failure affect performance reviews?
answer: A “meets most” rating helped him realize that the project needed to stop. He thinks a new manager’s fresh view was useful and that the performance process did its job.

He then helped every dependent team move to native code, React Native, or another chosen option, and deleted the framework completely. He did not leave a permanent remnant for someone else to maintain. He believes taking responsibility and publishing lessons gained goodwill afterward.

His advice is qualified: responsibly winding down a failed project can be better received than indefinitely dragging it out. This is his experience, not a guarantee about another organization’s evaluation.

followups.question: Were there signs you could have acted on earlier?
answer: For the last year he sensed that the project was going badly and sometimes lost sleep over it. His habitual response was to write more code and migrate more features. In retrospect, that treated an adoption and strategy problem as a coding shortage. He wishes he had accepted the signal earlier and found another useful problem.

blocks.question: How did you know management was wrong for you?
answer: He strongly prefers writing code and thinks he is better at communication tied to a concrete technical problem than at broader direction, documents, or organizational alignment. Managing would distance him from the part of the work he enjoys most. He describes himself as an extreme example and says the choice depends on the individual.

blocks.question: Why stay in iOS rather than switch domains?
answer: The path emerged rather than being planned. Reorganizations shifted his placement, but he liked the people, mobile work, and available opportunities. Staying let him acquire deep knowledge across the surrounding systems. He admires people who switch into areas such as AI or AR/VR and might choose differently as a new engineer today, but does not regret his own fit.

followups.question: Is depth or breadth better for reaching very senior IC levels?
answer: He sees multiple successful patterns and considers himself to have both. When GraphQL blocks his work, he investigates many layers of code instead of immediately handing the problem to its owners. He either fixes it or arrives with a precise diagnosis, saving them time and learning a new system. Repeating this problem-driven investigation builds broad, deep knowledge organically rather than through a predetermined checklist of systems.

blocks.question: How do you make sure your coding meets IC9 expectations?
answer: He stopped trying to judge each piece of code by its level. Instead, he regularly checks with his manager that he is solving important organizational problems and does work he enjoys. ComponentScript is his reminder that he can become attached to a direction that no longer matters; feedback should then cause him to listen and adjust. He does not advocate ignoring business relevance or management input.

blocks.question: What makes other senior engineers exceptional?
answer: Ernst admires several different strengths rather than one archetype: high-volume implementation, diagnosing unexplained metrics deep in unfamiliar systems, repeatedly starting complete useful projects, clear writing, and cross-team or cross-company alignment.

One colleague’s project-starting ability included not just code but deployment, documentation, naming, and multiple platforms. Other colleagues made complicated messages clear enough to become examples for engineers improving communication. He particularly respects a collaborator who manages the difficult Apple relationship—work Ernst lacks patience for himself.

The examples make complementarity explicit. A senior engineer who writes little code may still contribute through coordination that a productive implementer cannot supply. Several names are unclear in the captions, so the summary preserves their roles and contributions without inventing identities.

blocks.question: What would you tell yourself just after graduation?
answer: He would avoid changing a path that worked well for him. He nearly applied to Facebook in 2010 but discarded its puzzle-style process; joining later meant arriving at the native rewrite instead. He cannot know whether joining earlier would have been better. His broader advice is to find work one enjoys that intersects with industry needs, while recognizing the luck involved. Enjoying problem-solving does not mean every moment of debugging is pleasant; it supplies motivation for difficult work.

blocks.title: A working framework still needs an adoption strategy
rows: No clear audience between native and JavaScript developers.
Urgent feed stability and performance problem.
Infrastructure priorities imposed complexity some product teams did not value.
Concrete examples and allies supported adoption.
Scattered individual trials supplied too little team momentum.
